title: A child's hair
hook: combing a child's kesh, tying a small topknot and a patka
tomorrow: how do you teach a letter to a kid who can't read it yet?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first visit: no set count of days, because Guru Nanak called birth the Hukam, not a stain. Sehaj is home and sleeping. Little Fateh is wide awake.

Saturday morning, a cartoon on, a bottle of detangling spray, and a seven-year-old who has decided this is the worst day of his life. The whole family is busy with the new baby, so Simran is on hair duty for her little cousin Fateh. His hair has never been cut, and it reaches past his shoulders. Halfway through the first knot he shouts it: my friend Leo's hair is short and nobody combs it. Why can't I just cut mine? Simran stops, comb in the air. Two answers come to her at once.
screen: `SATURDAY, AND A TANGLE.` → `HAIR NEVER CUT.` → `"WHY CAN'T I JUST CUT IT?"`

segments.voice: Both answers live inside Sikh families, so let each one speak. The first: keep it from birth. Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five Ks, and the Sikh code of conduct asks parents to keep their children's hair uncut. Families who hold this say kesh isn't a decision a child makes at sixteen; it's simply who he is, the way he was made, from the first day. A small boy wears his hair in a joora, a topknot, often covered with a patka, a square of cloth tied over it, until he's ready for a full turban. The second: let him choose. Some Sikh families wait. Their best case is that a gift means most when it's chosen; they hope kesh will be his own yes, not a rule he resents. The code takes the first side, and Simran's family has too. But here's what both agree on, and it's the part that answers Fateh tonight. Nobody in either family wants hair to mean pain. The kanga, the small wooden comb a Sikh keeps in the hair, is about care, not war. Start from the ends. Hold the hair above the knot so it doesn't pull. Then the joora, and the patka tied neat on top.
screen: `KEEP IT FROM BIRTH: WHO HE IS.` · `LET HIM CHOOSE: HIS OWN YES.` · `BOTH AGREE: NOT PAIN.` · `THE KANGA: CARE, NOT WAR.` · then, large: `GENTLE HANDS.`

segments.voice: Take a comb or a brush to your own hair, or simply run your fingers through it. Go slowly, starting from the ends and working up, the way you'd comb a child who's tired of being combed. Then rest your hands in your lap for the sit.
Patka. A square of cloth tied over a child's topknot, worn before a full turban.
Gentle hands: whatever you think about the hair, the comb starts at the ends. That's today.
